1.goal: To open without saying what the object of the lesson is.
1.interaction: T–S, one line from you and straight on.
run: Do NOT announce that the lesson is about agreement. Stage 2 is diagnostic and only works if he does not know what you are measuring.
1.support: If he asks what today is about, say it is about the people around him at work, and move.
1.challenge: None here — anything extra tells him what you are measuring.
1.monitoring: Whether he tries to guess the target. If he does, move faster.
1.evidence: Nothing yet. The sample starts on the next screen.
1.transition: Move on when he is on the next screen.

2.goal: To take the baseline of the day, with no warning and no correction.
2.interaction: S speaks for thirty seconds; you write down his sentences.
run: Give the instruction below and let him talk.
Write HIS sentences down — the ones with a third-person error go into stage 4, mixed in with the correct ones.
CORRECT NOTHING HERE. Correcting now destroys both the measure and the discovery.
exact: Thirty seconds: who are the four people around you, and what does each one decide?
2.expected: Four people described, with the agreement holding or slipping — either way it is the measurement.
2.support: If he stops after two, ask who else he speaks to every week.
2.challenge: None here, for the same reason as the previous screen.
2.monitoring: Which sentences carry the third-person -s and which do not. You need both for stage 4.
2.evidence: His own sentences, written down. They are the material of the discovery stage.
2.transition: Move on when he has described the four.

3.goal: To hand him the content ready-made, so the difficulty sits only in the form.
3.interaction: S reads the chart; T–S on two questions.
run: Give him time to read the org chart.
Ask who would answer each of the last two questions from the pre-class — the two only he can answer.
The chart is a vehicle. Do not discuss the structure of his company here.
3.expected: The eight roles clear, and the two questions attributed to a person each.
3.support: If a role is unclear, ask what that person signs off on.
3.challenge: Ask which of the eight would be hardest to describe in one sentence.
3.monitoring: Whether the conversation drifts into his real org. Hold it: today the chart is scaffolding.
3.evidence: Whether the roles are clear enough to be spoken about without reading.
3.transition: Move on when the eight roles are clear.

4.goal: For HIM to find what separates the four right ones from the two wrong ones.
4.interaction: S marks on screen, then T–S until he words the difference.
run: Replace the sentences on screen with HIS OWN, collected at stage 2 and in lessons 1 and 2 — four correct, two with the error, without saying which.
He marks; then ask what is different about the two he did not mark. Wait. Do not give the rule.
If he says “I already know this”, answer once and move on: today is not about knowing it, it is about the form surviving a long sentence.
exact: What is different about the two you did not mark?
4.expected: The difference worded by him, however rough.
4.support: If the difference will not come, read one right and one wrong out loud, back to back, and ask what changed.
4.challenge: Ask him to write a seventh sentence with the same error on purpose.
4.monitoring: Whether he finds it in his own sentences. Finding it in someone else's is worth less.
4.evidence: His wording of the difference, and how many of his own errors he spotted.
4.transition: Move on when he has worded the difference.

5.goal: The whole form, once, in one line — AFTER his own attempt.
5.interaction: T shows and reads; S answers two CCQs.
run: Show it, read it, and leave. One minute, not five.
He already knows the rule. Explaining it again is what he complains about in teachers — the screen is there to check, not to teach.
exact: Does “the team” take the -s? (Yes, in American English: it is one group.) And “my partners and I”? (No: that is two people.)
5.support: If a CCQ misses, give the answer and move. This is not the stage to work it.
5.challenge: Ask about “everyone” and “none of them”, and take the answers quickly.
5.monitoring: Whether he treats the screen as new information. If he does, you are teaching what he already has.
5.evidence: Nothing new here — the measure is in the drill and in the free turn.
5.transition: Move on when the two CCQs are answered.

6.goal: Speed of retrieval of the form.
6.interaction: T gives the new subject; S redoes the sentence immediately. Twelve, fast.
run: Twelve sentences, fast. You give the new subject, he redoes the sentence.
Immediate, dry correction — one word: he wants. No explanation.
COUNT THE HITS. That number is half the evidence of the day; the other half comes from stage 8.
Do not stop halfway to explain.
6.expected: Twelve rebuilt sentences, with the hit count written down.
6.support: Shorten the prompt rather than explaining. The shorter the input, the faster the retrieval.
6.challenge: Alternate singular and plural subjects without warning.
6.monitoring: The hit rate, and whether it improves across the twelve.
6.evidence: The number of hits out of twelve. Half the evidence of the lesson.
6.transition: Move on when the twelve have gone by.

7.goal: His own sentences, with the chart still in view.
7.interaction: S says the eight, one at a time; you still correct.
run: He says the eight, one at a time, with his own content.
Here you still correct — it is the last stage where you do.
If he switches to the real names in his company, accept it: the real content is worth more.
7.expected: Eight sentences, one per person, each saying what that person decides.
7.support: If a sentence stalls, give the subject again and let him rebuild from there.
7.challenge: Ask for two of the eight joined into one sentence, with both subjects.
7.monitoring: Whether the form holds when the content is real and the sentence gets longer.
7.evidence: How the hit rate compares with the drill, before the chart comes off.
7.transition: Move on when the eight have come out.

8.goal: The production of the lesson — both sides of the table, ninety seconds, with nothing on screen.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are a partner who has never met any of these people.
run: CLOSE THE ORG CHART BEFORE HE STARTS.
Ninety seconds, both sides, nothing on screen.
DO NOT CORRECT DURING. Note the error rate — that rate, against the drill's, is the result of the lesson.
Record it.
8.expected: Eight roles described from memory, with the agreement holding more often than not.
8.support: If a name goes missing, give the role and let him continue. Do not give the sentence.
8.challenge: Ask one question about a person he did not mention and take the answer inside the ninety seconds.
8.monitoring: Whether he self-corrects on the move or stops the whole sentence to fix it. Both count, and they are different things.
8.evidence: The error rate in free speech, against the drill. That distance is exactly what he asked someone to measure, and it is the first time it exists as a number.
8.transition: Move on when he closes, or at ninety seconds.

9.goal: To hand back two points and to ask for the same eight in half the time.
9.interaction: T–S, two short points, then one retask.
run: Two things, short and direct.
Then: the same eight roles, forty-five seconds, focused on what each one DECIDES.
GIVE HIM THE TWO NUMBERS OUT LOUD — hits in the drill and hits in free speech. The distance between them is what he asked someone to measure.
Do not add content. The retask is the same task under one changed constraint.
exact: Same eight, forty-five seconds — and your partner only wants to know what each one decides.
9.expected: The same eight with the descriptions gone and the decisions kept.
9.support: If forty-five seconds will not fit, ask which two of the eight the partner does not need.
9.challenge: Ask for it once more in twenty seconds and see which four survive.
9.monitoring: Whether the agreement holds when the sentences get shorter and faster.
9.evidence: The two numbers, said out loud and written in the record.
9.transition: Move on when the forty-five seconds have been given.

10.goal: To register what was worked on and to leave the next lesson announced.
10.interaction: S ticks the list; T–S on the close.
run: He ticks what he recognizes.
Homework, said out loud and never on screen: the post-class has one optional recording about his real team and a reference page for the form, to check when it slips.
Announce lesson 4: it closes the block — three minutes presenting the company to Diane, and two questions he has not seen.
exact: Lesson 4 is the real meeting: three minutes on your company, and two questions you have not seen. Everything from these three lessons goes in with you.
10.expected: Some lines ticked, and one honest answer on the confidence row.
10.support: If nothing is ticked, read the two numbers back to him and ask which one he wants to move.
10.challenge: Ask which of the eight people he will describe in English this week, and to whom.
10.monitoring: Whether the confidence mark tracks the drill number or the free-speech one. The gap is the lesson.
10.evidence: Fill the post-lesson record BEFORE you close. The next lesson reads the four together and steers the planning that follows.
